study.title: Ephesians 1 Blessings in Christ, inheritance, and the church as the body of Christ
study.overview: Ephesians 1 opens the letter with a greeting that already highlights the will of God, the identity of the holy people, and the grace and peace coming from the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Then Paul blesses God for all that he has bestowed in Christ: choice before the foundation of the world, adoption as children, redemption by blood, forgiveness of sins, revelation of his plan and seal of the Holy Spirit. The chapter ends with a prayer for believers to understand more deeply the hope, the inheritance and power of God, power seen in the resurrection and exaltation of Christ, which was placed as the head of the church, his body.

outline.title: Greeting and Early Blessing
outline.explanation: Paul presents himself as an apostle by the will of God and addresses the letter to the saints and faithful in Christ. The salutation invokes grace and peace and soon unfolds in praise to God for having blessed believers with spiritual blessings in Christ. This section underlines the divine choice, the desired holiness and adoption as children, all to the praise of God's grace.

outline.title: Redemption, revelation and seal of the Spirit
outline.explanation: Here Paul describes the center of saving work: in Christ there is deliverance for the blood and forgiveness of sins. God also revealed the mystery of his will, summed up in the gathering of all things in Christ in due time. Believers, upon hearing and believing in the gospel, were sealed with the Holy Spirit, who is a guarantee of the future inheritance until the final redemption.

outline.title: Prayer for understanding and exaltation of Christ
outline.explanation: Paul thanks for the faith and love of the readers and prays that they may receive wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of God. He asks enlightened eyes to understand divine hope, inheritance, and power. This power was demonstrated in the resurrection and enthronement of Christ above all government and authority, and God made him head over all things to the church, which is his body.

study.context: The notes indicate that Paul follows the common pattern of the ancient Greek letters, but the Christianizes in linking his authorship to the divine call, salute the recipients as saints and faithful and invoking grace and peace. There is also an important textual observation: some ancient manuscripts do not bring the expression 'in Ephesus', and Adam Clarke's note mentions that some scholars thought the letter might have had another fate, although this is presented as textual discussion and not as certainty. The name Ephesus, in Clarke's notes, is associated with an important city in Asia Minor, but this information should be used with caution, as the letter's own address issue appears as debated.
study.theology: The chapter presents a robust theology of God's sovereignty and the centrality of Christ. Salvation is shown as divine initiative: God chooses, predestines, adopts, redeems, reveals and seals. At the same time, the real human response appears in hearing the word of truth and believing in the gospel. The text also teaches that the work of Christ is not only individual: the ultimate purpose is to gather all things in him. The church emerges as a reality marked by the Spirit, sustained by hope and defined by the union with Christ, his head. The language of 'mystery' does not point to something esoteric, but to the divine plan previously hidden and now revealed in Christ. Paul's prayer shows that spiritual knowledge is not mere information, but an understanding enlightened by the Spirit, leading to confidence in the hope and praise of the glory of God.

scholarViews.insight: The repeated emphasis on God's will highlights his sovereignty in fulfilling his plan, especially at the beginning of the letter.
Paul begins with gratitude and praise for the spiritual blessings given through Jesus Christ, transforming the opening of the letter into adoration.
The expression "in wisdom and prudence" is understood as instruction given by the Spirit and practical discernment to preach the gospel effectively.

questions: How does repeated emphasis on God's will shape the way you understand your identity in Christ and your spiritual security?
In what way has the fact that it has been "sealed with the Holy Spirit" changes its vision of hope, perseverance and future?
If Christ is head over all things to the church, what should this alter in community life and in his personal obedience today?
study.practice: Set aside time to turn Ephesians 1 into prayer: thank God for blessings in Christ, confess your dependence on the Spirit to understand the gospel and ask spiritual eyes to perceive God's hope, inheritance, and power. Then practice this in a concrete way seeking a specific attitude of love for another Christian, since true faith in Christ is expressed in love for the saints. Finally, he rereads the letter by remembering that the church is not the center, but the body of Christ, and that his life should reflect his authority.
study.uncertainty: There is textual uncertainty as to the expression 'in Ephesus' in verse 1, because the notes record that important ancient manuscripts do not include it. There is also interpretive divergence in the notes on the exact meaning of 'fullness' in 1:23: Tyndale emphasizes the church as full expression of Christ in the world, while Adam Clarke points out that Christ fills the church with spiritual gifts; both are interpretive readings, not closed definitions of the text.
